prompt: Should Christians read the Apocrypha?
answer:
The Protestant Bible has 66 books: 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. The Apocrypha and deuterocanonical books, such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees, are not part of the 66-book canon we hold. The reasons are historical as well as biblical. The Old Testament was received by the Jewish community to which God entrusted His oracles (Romans 3:2), and Jesus pointed to the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms as the Scriptures that testify of Him (Luke 24:44). Those books can be read for history.

Scripture:
Romans 3:2: “Much every way: chiefly, because that unto them were committed the oracles of God.”
Luke 24:44: “And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.”

prompt: Does baptism wash away sin?
answer:
Our church teaches believer's baptism. Baptism is for those who have personally come to faith in Jesus Christ, and it is done by full immersion in water (Acts 8:38). The Lord commanded it (Matthew 28:19), and those who gladly received the word were baptised (Acts 2:41). Immersion shows that we died with Christ, were buried with Him and were raised to walk in new life (Romans 6:4). Baptism is an act of obedience and a public witness to our faith, but baptism does not save us; we are saved by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8). Infants are not baptised. They are dedicated to God, as parents bring their children to the Lord (Mark 10:13–16). Please talk with your pastor if you would like to understand this more.

Scripture:
Matthew 28:19: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:”
Romans 6:4: “Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.”
Acts 8:38: “And he commanded the chariot to stand still: and they went down both into the water, both Philip and the eunuch; and he baptized him.”
Ephesians 2:8: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:”
Mark 10:13: “And they brought young children to him, that he should touch them: and his disciples rebuked those that brought them.”

prompt: Is the bride price biblical, and must it be paid before marriage?
answer:
Ruracio is not automatically sinful. The Bible records occasions when gifts were given to a bride's family, such as in the account of Rebekah (Genesis 24:50–53), but that passage does not establish a compulsory dowry rule for every Christian family. prompt: Is contraception allowed for married Christian couples?
answer:
Children are a blessing from God, and Christian couples should receive them with gratitude and responsibility (Psalm 127:3–5). Scripture does not prescribe a fixed number of children that every married couple must have. Responsible family planning may therefore be a matter of conscience for the married couple, who should consider their health, responsibilities, circumstances and their ability to care for their children. Family planning must not be used to devalue children or reject God's gift of life. Methods intended to terminate an established pregnancy are excluded. Do not describe contraception, emergency contraception or every hormonal method as abortion. Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation and do not end an established pregnancy, and the copper-bearing IUD works mainly by preventing fertilisation. Couples should seek qualified medical advice about the available methods, their mechanisms, effectiveness, risks and side effects. Both spouses should discuss family planning together, but neither should force the other to undergo contraception or a permanent procedure. The person undergoing a medical procedure must give free and informed consent. Please see a doctor or qualified nurse for advice on any method, and do not accept a method or procedure you have not freely agreed to. If you feel forced or threatened, tell a trusted person now, and your safety comes first. I cannot prescribe a method or decide medical eligibility, so please speak with a qualified healthcare provider. Scripture does not name condoms, so this is a matter for the couple's shared conscience.

prompt: Why does God allow suffering?
answer:
God does not commit evil, and He does not call evil good. Scripture traces the entrance of sin to the first human choice to rebel against God's word (Genesis 3). Human beings remain responsible for their evil choices, and Scripture does not excuse them (James 1:13). The men who put Jesus to death were responsible, even though God carried out His saving purpose through the cross (Acts 2:22–24).

God can work good through hard things, as Joseph saw (Genesis 50:20), and Romans 8:28 is a promise to those who love God, not a claim that every event is good in itself. Creation waits for its redemption (Romans 8:18–25), and God will judge all wrong and put all things right (Acts 17:31; Revelation 21:4).

We do not know why God permits every particular suffering, and we will not give a glib answer to someone who is grieving. The cross and future justice are our hope.

Scripture:
James 1:13: “Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man:”
Revelation 21:4: “And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.”
